title: Ghosts at Little Rock's MacArthur Museum tell paranormal investigators to 'get out'

content:
LITTLE ROCK (KATV) — The Tower Building of the Little Rock Arsenal, now home to the MacArthur Museum of Arkansas Military History, has been described as one of the most haunted places in the South. For that reason, on this week's episode of Spirits of Arkansas.

The Tower Building the MacArthur Museum calls home was Arkansas' first arsenal and is nearly as old as the state itself. With such a long history, it's no surprise that the past doesn't stay dead here.

The arsenal was built in 1840 to establish a U.S. military presence in the newly founded state of Arkansas.

"The governor requested funds from the federal government to build a military post here on these grounds to protect Arkansans from enemy attack," said Stephen McAteer, director of the MacArthur Museum of Arkansas Military History.

During the Civil War, it fell under Confederate control until 1863, when the Union recaptured it.

In 1864, 17-year-old David Dodd, one of the spirits said to haunt the property, was hanged near the arsenal for spying on the Union Army.

Until it was decommissioned in 1890, the arsenal served more as a housing complex for soldiers. Douglas MacArthur, the museum's namesake, was born there in 1880. By an act of Congress, the former arsenal grounds were turned into Little Rock's first public park.

After spending decades empty, in 1942, the building became home to the Museum of Natural History and Antiquities, founded by suffragette and writer Bernie Babcock. One of the more notable displays was an over 2,000-year-old mummy that remained there until the late '90s, when the Museum of Natural History relocated and the current museum was established.

"We came on board in 1999. I was hired to work with the city to create a new museum that we now have as the MacArthur Museum of Arkansas Military History," McAteer told KATV.

Since the '90s, the museum has gained a reputation for being haunted.

"All the relics ... guns and everything it's in the museum right now ... all that carries energy," said Rhonda Burton, co-founder of Arkansas Ghost Catchers.

In 2011, Burton, a paranormal investigator, approached McAteer with the idea of holding a paranormal expo as a fundraiser — something that has become an annual event drawing Bigfoot, UFO and ghost enthusiasts.

"If it gets them here, it gets the building additional publicity, then the museum benefits from that ... So we appreciate Rhonda and the efforts that she does for the Expo," McAteer said.

And though he hasn't experienced anything spooky, McAteer says his staff have.

"Some of my staff have felt a presence ... the sound of soldiers dragging boxes. The building initially was an ammunition warehouse, so it would not have been uncommon for them to move boxes of ammunition from floor to floor," McAteer said.

And that's not all. Guests and staff have reported seeing apparitions. One of them is a woman in a white dress standing on the staircase landing.

Some believe the reason the museum is so active is because of séances held in the basement by Bernie Babcock, the writer and suffragette who founded the Museum of Natural History in 1942.

"People believe that that's what's happened. They held these séances and maybe opened a door ... and that's why there's so much going on," Burton told KATV.

Burton has conducted many paranormal investigations in the museum. During an investigation in the building's tower, her team recorded an ominous electronic voice phenomenon, or EVP, on a microphone. It appears to say, "Get out."

"When I heard that I was shocked. It was like, oh my gosh, you gotta be kidding me," Burton said.

The MacArthur Museum's Paranormal Expo will be held Oct. 24-25.
